lesson.title: Peak Value: How High a Waveform Actually Climbs
lesson.summary: The peak value is the single highest instantaneous magnitude a waveform reaches, a quantity that matches the amplitude for a plain sinusoid but can diverge from it the moment a signal carries a DC offset.
lesson.body:
The peak value of a waveform, written Vm or Im, is the maximum instantaneous value the signal reaches, measured from the zero axis, not from wherever the waveform happens to sit on average. For a textbook sinusoid v(t) = Vm sin(omega t + theta), the peak value and the amplitude Vm are literally the same number, because that pure sine wave is centered symmetrically around zero with no vertical shift.

The two ideas split apart as soon as a DC offset enters the picture. Consider v(t) = 5 + 3 sin(omega t) volts. The amplitude, the coefficient in front of the sine term, is still 3 V, since that is how far the signal swings above and below its own center. But the peak value, the highest point the waveform actually reaches, is 5 + 3 = 8 V, and there is also a distinct negative peak of 5 - 3 = 2 V. Amplitude describes the size of the swing; peak value describes the highest altitude reached, and only when the center sits at zero do those two numbers coincide.

A standard North American wall outlet is rated at 120 V, and that number is a root mean square value, not a peak value. To find the peak, multiply the RMS value by the square root of 2: Vm = Vrms times sqrt(2) = 120 times 1.41421 = 169.71 V. So although the outlet is described as 120 volts, the voltage actually climbs to nearly 170 V at the top of every single cycle, and swings down to nearly negative 170 V at the bottom. This factor of sqrt(2) between RMS and peak is specific to sinusoids and comes directly from how RMS is defined as an averaged square value.

Peak value is what determines whether a component survives, since insulation breakdown, diode reverse voltage ratings, and capacitor voltage ratings all care about the highest instantaneous stress a device will see, not the average or RMS value. A capacitor rated for only 150 V would be destroyed by that same 120 V RMS outlet, precisely because the actual peak of 169.71 V exceeds its rating, even though the RMS value looks perfectly safe on paper.

This same sqrt(2) relationship is captured by a quantity called crest factor, the ratio of peak value to RMS value. For any pure sinusoid, crest factor is always sqrt(2), about 1.414, regardless of amplitude or frequency. An ideal square wave, by contrast, sits at its extreme value the entire time, so its RMS value equals its peak value exactly, giving a crest factor of 1. Waveforms with sharp, narrow spikes, like some switching power supply currents, can have a crest factor of 3 or more, meaning their peak value is far higher than their RMS value would suggest, a mismatch that catches out anyone who sizes a component using RMS current alone.

Amplitude, the prerequisite idea behind this one, is best thought of as the size of the oscillation itself, how far the signal swings from its own center. Peak value takes that same swing and asks where it lands relative to true zero. For any signal without a DC offset, including most of the sinusoidal sources used in early circuit analysis, the distinction is invisible and the two words get used interchangeably, but the moment a real circuit adds a bias voltage, the two numbers can differ by exactly the size of that offset.
